1.pericope_label: Afterward he brought me to the temple, and measured the posts, six cubits broad on the one side, and six cubits broad on the other side, which was the breadth of the tabernacle
debates: How the six cubits of the first verse and the five of the second are reconciled
Whether the wall dividing the two rooms is measured at all
Whether this temple and the earlier one are on the same plan
What the temple of the vision stands for
outliers: Ellicott resolves the discrepancy by taking the first measurement the other way, of the thickness of the side walls, and notes that the supplied words give a false impression
Henry takes the same clause the opposite way, reckoning the posts twelve cubits apart so that the door itself equalled the breadth of the tabernacle
Clarke infers from the identity of the dimensions with those of Solomon’s sanctuary that the two were on the same plan and the later meant as an exact resemblance
Henry holds the vision has a joint respect to the second temple, to the body of Christ and to the church, which is why an ambiguous saying about destroying the temple was possible

Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch both observe that the angel enters the holy of holies alone, Ellicott because under the law the prophet might not, Delitzsch because the verb is he went in and not he brought me
Delitzsch refers the third verse to the partition wall and reads its six cubits, with Kliefoth, as a height, where Ellicott holds the partition nowhere measured at all
themes: A priest compensated for a lost birthright by a vision
A dividing wall measured by one witness and declared unmeasured by another
Walls as thick as the whole breadth of the older tabernacle
A door that overlaps its posts by half a cubit on each side
A word for temple narrowed to the nave alone

5.pericope_label: And the side chambers were three, one over another, and thirty in order; and they entered into the wall which was of the house for the side chambers round about
debates: Whether a space stood between the side chambers and the wall of the house
What the great cubits are measured to
How the storeys of chambers widened
outliers: Ellicott rejects the Greek version that puts a space between the chambers and the wall, since it is inconsistent with the original and would require an inner wall of which nothing is said
Ellicott rules out the armpit-cubit, since no such measure is known and the prophet has already fixed his cubit, and takes the word as joint, the point where superstructure meets foundation
Gill sets the floors at four, five and six cubits while Wesley gives five, six and seven for the chambers
Ellicott admits the description of the enlarging is difficult and cannot be pressed further without settling words whose meaning is disputed
themes: Massiveness said to be carried to excess to signify security
Beams resting on ledges rather than set into the wall
An exact square recovered by adding the parts across and lengthwise
Chambers widening as the church nears the heavenly state

12.pericope_label: Now the building that was before the separate place at the end toward the west was seventy cubits broad; and the wall of the building was five cubits thick round about
debates: What the western building was for
Which building the thirteenth verse means
outliers: Henry admits we are not told the use of the building and guesses it signifies a church among the Gentiles of quite another nature than the Jewish temple
Ellicott guesses instead that it is the appointed place named later for burning the sin-offering and other refuse from the temple
Gill takes the separate place for the holy of holies, Clarke for the temple itself, and Ellicott for the twenty-cubit space at the west end
Delitzsch derives the term from a verb meaning to cut, so that it names ground cut off, the same word serving for a desert no road reaches
Clarke reaches ninety cubits by one itemised reckoning and a hundred and one by another
Wesley takes the building of the thirteenth verse to be what flanks the temple north and south, not the structure to the west
Ellicott says the word for galleries occurs only here and three times more, that its derivation is quite unknown, and that they cannot be placed on the plan
themes: A building guessed to be a church and guessed to be an incinerator
A name that means simply what has been cut off
A word whose derivation is admitted to be quite unknown
A total of a hundred and one cubits reached by itemised addition
A passage of ten cubits left on each side

16.pericope_label: And it was made with cherubims and palm trees, so that a palm tree was between a cherub and a cherub; and every cherub had two faces
debates: Why they have two faces here and four elsewhere
outliers: Gill takes the cherubim not for angels but for the ministers of the word, distinguished on one side from angels and on the other from ordinary Christians
Ellicott explains the two faces by saying the cherubim are symbolic rather than actual creatures and may be modified at pleasure, here to suit the exigencies of the carving
Ellicott admits the thick planks are extremely doubtful, the word occurring elsewhere only once, and suggests a moulding of wood
Ellicott corrects door posts to thresholds, narrow windows to closed windows, and removes stories as not in the original
themes: Light described as narrow without and broad within
A door wider than the state it prefigures
Planks thick enough for figures carved in relief
Almost everything in the building made foursquare
